findings.message: Paragraph 3 says the marks went down from the Tower to a crack in the wall and something 'had been hiding in the wall since'. In lantern-room paragraph 4 the crab is found behind the small drum at the top, so the crack and the 'hiding in the wall' line do not match. Pick one place for the hiding spot, or say the crab went back up.

Paragraph 1 lines the lunch box with 'his scarf from his bag'. No scarf or bag was set up earlier. Paragraph 5 also puts two speakers (Lira and Eli) in one paragraph, which is hard to follow for a struggling reader. Split it into two paragraphs.
Paragraph 4 refers to 'Lira's warm scarf', which was never mentioned. Introduce it earlier (for example in meet-lira) or drop it.

Paragraph 4 sets up 'a tall hook hung by the hatch lid' but no choice uses it. The reed net route (net-lid) and the ladder route (ladder-climb) both end at lantern-room with no difference in outcome, so the net item and the frog choice do not change which endings can be reached. This is a loose clue, not a defect.

The validation report's brief block warns that 3 sentences exceed the brief's 16-word limit (validation.r2.json, brief.warnings). The report does not name them. The author should find them and shorten them.

A child falls down an open manhole and is unhurt. It is gentle and fantasy framed, and it is not violence. A parent may still want to know that the story shows a child following an animal into a manhole. Flagged for the parent stage only.

The clue chain that gates the best ending contradicts itself. In 'the-stairs' the claw marks 'came down from the Tower and ran to a crack in the wall'. In 'the-prints' the reader is told something 'had left the Tower in a hurry, and been hiding in the wall since'. But in 'lantern-room' the crab is at the top of the Tower behind the small drum, and the text says 'The wet marks on the stairs had come from here.' A reader who follows the clue is led to expect a creature in the wall, then finds it upstairs, so the inference is muddled exactly where 'offer-den' (requires claw-prints) depends on it. Ask the narrative designer to make the marks and the crab's hiding place agree (for example, marks lead UP to the Tower, or the crab is seen going back up).

Contradiction about what Eli saw. In 'the-marsh' the narration says of the stuck frog 'Only Eli did' see it, and Eli chooses to hop on. In 'stone-hop' it says 'Eli did not see it.' That reads as an error and may confuse a reader tracking who knows what. Suggest 'Eli did not look back' or similar.

Unestablished object and speaker confusion. 'He lined it with his scarf from his bag' introduces a scarf and bag that Eli was never given (continuity lists only a lunch box and library book). In the same paragraph Lira says 'Maybe you are the hero' and Eli replies ('I am just a boy who followed a cat') with no paragraph break, which makes speaker tracking harder for a reader with dyslexia. Split into two paragraphs. 'two-heads' also adds 'Lira's warm scarf' without setup.

Ending recalls the frog on every route. 'He looked at his muddy shoes and thought of the frog, the stairs and the dark hatch.' A child who took the 'hop-stones' path never helped the frog and was told 'Eli did not see it'. Consider 'thought of the marsh' so the line is true on both routes.

Glossary 'promised' (defined as 'Told that something would happen for sure') does not match its only use in the text, 'Eli promised to visit' in 'ending-two-heads', which means 'gave his word'. The sense in the definition appears only in the premise, which the child does not read in play. Either use the word in the 'meet-lira' prophecy ('a hero who was promised') or change the definition.

Word-set fit, observed by reading the draft: every blend-set word (step, stone, frog, plan, spin, trip, crab, drum) opens with a consonant blend; every closed-syllable word (cat, map, net, lid, hop, mud, bus) is a single short vowel closed by a consonant; every ing word (running, jumping, hiding, climbing, glowing, ringing) is a base plus -ing. Notes for the parent's program: 'stone' is a blend word but also a silent-e word, not a closed syllable; 'running' doubles the consonant and 'hiding' drops the silent e, so the ing set mixes three spelling conventions. These are fine for ages 10 to 13 but should be mapped deliberately. All words appear on every route (report: blend 11 to 22, closed-syllable 19 to 28, ing 8 to 12 per ending route, against minimums of 10, 8 and 8). Most uses read naturally; 'gave a hop' / 'gave a small hop' / 'made a big hop' is repeated enough to read as drilling in 'through-the-gap', 'the-gate' and 'frog-helped'.

Limits of the automated report, which this review relies on only partly. Detection is by spelling, not sound. The 'Suffix -ing' count of 34 includes 'anything' and 'nothing', which are not the suffix. The closed-syllable count of 786 and the 'ea' in 'bread' type matches overcount. The report does not judge decodability, vocabulary or story quality. This AI review is not a certified literacy review. Reading level, age fit and decodability judgements are mine from the text; I did not test with a reader.

Skills practised: reading this story, a child decodes in context short words with consonant blends (step, frog, trip, crab, drum), closed-syllable words (cat, map, mud, hop) and -ing words (running, climbing, glowing, ringing), meeting each often on every route. They follow cause and effect and sequence through the fall, the marsh and the climb, infer from clues (the wet marks, the shivering crab) and the choices that depend on them, track who is speaking in dialogue, and pick up vocabulary from context (lantern, marsh, hatch, creature). The age fit for 10 to 13 is good: short sentences (average 8.1 words), no violence, and a theme of kindness and courage that does not talk down.

Logic gap: the reader opens the hatch lid with the net from the floor, then 'climbed through the hatch' with no ladder. The hatch is high above the hall (tower-hall paragraph 2), and the ladder is only used on the other route. Add a line about using the ladder, or say the net pulled the lid down on a rope.

Continuity: Eli lines the lunch box 'with soft moss from the stairs' but never picks up any moss (he is not shown taking it). He also leaves the lunch box with the crab and goes home without it, which is not mentioned.

Unclear referent: 'They climbed the stairs, one by one ... Each one shone with a speck of glow dust.' Paragraph 3 is about the marks, so 'each one' reads as the stairs or the marks. A reader with dyslexia may stumble. Say 'Each mark shone ...'.

Safety tone: both openings have the child lean over an open manhole to look down (choices lean-over and lean-over-gate). It is the premise, and the landing is soft, but a child may copy it. Consider one line that says it was a foolish thing to do or that this is a story-world fall.

Pronoun is unclear. 'They climbed the stairs, one by one, toward the Tower. Each one shone with a speck of glow dust.' Just before this, 'They were like little claws' means the marks, but 'They climbed' reads as Eli, Lira and Ash. 'Each one shone' then has no clear referent. Suggest 'The marks climbed the stairs, one by one, toward the Tower. Each one shone...' (narrative designer's call).

The brief sets maxSentenceWords 16. By my count, 'Eli's library book had a map in it, and he was meant to show it in class.' is 17 words. The report only flags sentences over 20, so it did not catch this. Splitting at 'and' would fit the limit and help a slower decoder.

Small logic wobble in the setup of the missing stone. 'The glow stone lived up there. It had gone missing three nights ago.' says the stone is up there and also missing. The lantern room later shows the crab holding it, so the facts agree, but a first-time reader has to repair them. Consider 'The glow stone should be up there, but it had gone missing three nights ago.' In 'lantern-room', 'Whatever was in the Tower's heart was not a villain' is also an abstract phrase for the age; 'The thing in the Tower was not a villain' is clearer.

Repeated 'gave a ...' frame: 'gave a hop' (late-for-school), 'gave a little trip' (the-gate), 'gave a spin, a trip and a splash' (stone-hop), 'gave a creak' (ladder-climb), 'gave a loud croak and made a big hop' (frog-helped), 'gave a small, surprised smile' (frog-helped), 'gave a small, sad squeak' (ending-the-grab). It is far better than in revision 2, but it still leans on this frame to carry the blend words 'hop', 'trip' and 'spin'. 'gave a little trip' is the least natural; 'gave a little trip' could be 'tripped a little' or 'nearly tripped'. Not a blocker.

shelfSummary.blurb: A gentle fantasy adventure in which a boy follows a cat into a land whose tower light is fading. It practises beginning blends, closed syllables and -ing endings, with sequencing, inference and vocabulary from context.

findings.message: The new branch choice added to fix the single-choice error is not a genuine branch, and it contradicts the passage it leads to. how-to-go-down (story.r6.json lines 106-117, tagged learningTargets ['sequencing','engagement']) offers 'Jump in fast, feet first' (jump-in-fast, line 114) versus 'Ease yourself down slowly instead' (go-down-slow, line 115) -- both deliberate, different actions -- but both target the-fall, whose opening line (line 166) is 'The rim was wet. Eli's shoe slid, and down he went.' That is an accidental slip, not a deliberate jump or a slow, controlled descent. A reader who picks either new choice gets a next page that denies the choice they just made. This also undercuts the 'sequencing' learning target the passage is tagged with. Fix: either give the-fall two short variant openings keyed to how he went down, or rewrite the two new choice labels/outcomes so they are consistent with 'his shoe slid' (e.g. both describe different flavors of the same slip) rather than implying full control.

Same contradiction as how-to-go-down. last-look-at-the-gate (lines 150-161) offers 'Trust the cat and climb down' (trust-the-cat, line 158), which explicitly describes a controlled climb, and 'Decide to follow the cat anyway' (go-anyway, line 159); both target the-fall, whose text (line 166) is an accidental slide ('his shoe slid, and down he went'), not a climb. 'trust-the-cat' in particular reads as a deliberate, careful descent and is flatly contradicted by the next passage. Needs the same fix approach as how-to-go-down: either branch the-fall's opening or rewrite the choice outcome so it does not promise a controlled climb that never happens.

Minor, not blocking: watch-the-hill (lines 235-246) offers 'Wave first, before she gets close' (wave-first) vs 'Wait quietly for her to speak' (wait-quiet), both targeting meet-lira. meet-lira's text (lines 248-263) has Lira speak first regardless ('"That is Ash," she said'), with no acknowledgement of whether Eli waved. Not a hard contradiction since the two can coexist, but the choice has no visible effect on the following text, so it reads as cosmetic rather than a genuine branch. Same pattern (a choice with no visible narrative effect) appears in several of the round-2 connector passages added in this revision (watch-the-frog-hop, look-back-at-the-marsh, last-step-up, steady-your-nerves, one-more-breath, settle-in-the-mud) -- none of these have continuity errors like how-to-go-down/last-look-at-the-gate, but none of them change any text, item, clue or ending outcome either. They satisfy the graph validator's 'at least two choices' rule, but most are decorative forks that immediately rejoin with no acknowledgement of which fork was taken. Worth a narrative pass to give at least a couple of these a one-clause callback in the passage they rejoin, so the extra choices read as real decisions rather than validator filler.

I ran `npm run check` myself (lint, typecheck, 191 unit tests, validate:stories, agents:check, build). Lint, typecheck, tests and build all passed. `npm run validate:stories` FAILED overall (exit code 1): it reports 'public/stories/previews/the-cat-who-took-the-wrong-turn.json: schema: ok; graph: 9 error(s), 0/5 endings reachable' with the same nine single-choice passage ids this job's r5/r6 fixed (through-the-gap, the-gate, the-fall, varro, frog-helped, stone-hop, the-prints, net-lid, ladder-climb). That file is a stale, separate demo/preview snapshot at story version 4 (checked with grep), not the job's draft; it is unrelated to narrative-designer's work on this job and I did not and must not edit it per my task's scope (no touching public/stories/previews). The same validate:stories run also fails on four other, unrelated jobs' stale preview snapshots (the-derelict-salvage, the-rain-courier, the-tomb-of-ameru, wake-cycle), so this looks like a pre-existing, repo-wide staleness issue, not something introduced by this revision. I am reporting the real `npm run check` output rather than claiming a pass: as of this review, `npm run check` does not pass for the repository as a whole, for reasons outside this job's draft. This should be escalated (orchestrator/release-manager) separately from this story's content review. The job's own automated-validation gate (reports/validation.r6.json) is ok: true, schema ok, graph ok with 5/5 endings reachable, which I verified directly against the r6 draft.

Routes traced against story.r6.json and graph.r6.json (choice ids; item/clue gates checked): (1) ending-warm-den (triumph, requires clue claw-prints): late-for-school--squeeze-through-->through-the-gap--lean-over-->the-fall--look-around-->varro--meet-lira-->meet-lira--take-stairs-->the-stairs--study-prints-->the-prints [+claw-prints]--up-after-prints-->tower-hall--climb-ladder-->ladder-climb--up-ladder-->lantern-room--offer-den (clue held)-->ending-warm-den. (2) ending-drum-song (triumph): any route to lantern-room--tap-drum-->ending-drum-song. (3) ending-the-grab (bittersweet): lantern-room--grab-stone-->ending-the-grab. (4) ending-two-heads (triumph): lantern-room--ask-lira-->ending-two-heads. (5) ending-home-too-soon (setback, no items needed): late-for-school--try-the-gate-->the-gate--lean-over-gate-->the-fall--check-bag-->check-the-book--stand-after-check-->varro--look-moss-->look-at-the-moss--wave-after-moss-->meet-lira--take-marsh-->the-marsh--hop-stones-->stone-hop--to-stairs-fast-->the-stairs--keep-climbing-->tower-hall--ask-home-->home-too-soon. All five endings are reachable this way, matching graph.r6.json's reachableEndings. The reed-net item (granted only by frog-helped, line 288) correctly gates the locked net-the-lid choice in tower-hall, with a fair lockedHint ('You need something light and woven to catch the lid.', line 440) that matches the item's description. The claw-prints clue (granted only by the-prints, line 389) correctly gates the locked offer-den choice in lantern-room, with a fair lockedHint ('Think about the small wet marks you saw on the stairs.', line 549). No item or clue is referenced before it is granted, and no route backtracks through a passage already read (every edge in graph.r6.json moves forward through the late-for-school -> through-the-gap/the-gate -> the-fall -> varro -> meet-lira -> marsh/stairs -> tower-hall -> lantern-room -> ending spine, with the new connector/second-choice detours rejoining the same spine rather than looping back).

Content integrity and literacy word sets: the story reads as original, age-appropriate content with no violence, real brands, romance or religion, matching the brief's 'avoid' list; the crab reveal in lantern-room (lines 536-540) is gentle (cold and shivering, not a villain), consistent across all four lantern-room endings. Characters (Eli, Ash, Lira, the Lantern Tower) and facts (land of Varro, Eli wants to go home) match brief.json's continuity block. reports/validation.r6.json confirms all three word sets meet their minOccurrences and appear on the shortest route to every ending (word-sets-on-every-route: ok), and all three target concepts (initial-blend, closed-syllable, suffix-ing) are present with no concept mismatches. Pre-existing, non-blocking: three sentences carried over unchanged since revision 4 are one word over the brief's 16-word maxSentenceWords (not the automated 20-word hard limit): late-for-school line 67 ('Eli's library book had a map in it, and he was meant to show it in class.' -- 17 words), frog-helped line 286 ('She was waiting at the start of the stairs, and she gave him a small, surprised smile.' -- 17 words), and home-too-soon line 625 ('He looked at his muddy shoes and thought of the marsh, the stairs and the dark hatch.' -- 17 words). These were already flagged as minor by the r4 literacy review and are outside this revision's scope (single-choice fixes only); flagging again for the literacy stage, not as a QA blocker.

The round-2 fix (r6) added nine small passages so every r5 connector would itself have two choices: how-to-go-down, last-look-at-the-gate, settle-in-the-mud, watch-the-hill, watch-the-frog-hop, look-back-at-the-marsh, last-step-up, steady-your-nerves, one-more-breath. Together with the nine r5 connectors (call-to-the-cat, call-for-help, check-the-book, look-at-the-moss, thank-the-frog, careful-hop, show-lira-the-prints, check-on-ash, help-lira-up), that is 18 new passages. I read all 18 against the three word sets: only 'look-at-the-moss' contains an ing-word-set word ('glowing', 'running'); the other 17 contain none of running/jumping/hiding/climbing/glowing/ringing. Two passages, 'how-to-go-down' and 'watch-the-hill', contain no word-set word from any of the three sets at all. I then enumerated every complete start-to-ending path through the r6 graph by script (132,224 paths, respecting the reed-net/claw-prints gates) and summed word-set occurrences per path. The brief's minimums (blend 10, closed-syllable 8, ing 8) are still met on every single path I found (worst case: blend 10, closed-syllable 21, ing 9), so this is not an automated-check failure and not a 'missing from a route' failure. But the margin on suffix-ing is now thin (9 against a floor of 8) specifically because of this new content, and one of only three target concepts in the brief is carried almost entirely by pre-existing r4 material rather than by any of the passages r6 added. I recommend the narrative designer weave at least a couple of ing-set words into a few of these 18 passages (several have an easy, natural fit, see next finding) rather than leaving them as pure structural filler.

'watch-the-hill' (new in r6) actually removes a pattern-practice opportunity rather than adding one. The passages on either side of it both use the exact ing-set word for this scene: 'varro' has the choice label 'Wave to the girl running down the hill', and the passage this new one branches off, 'look-at-the-moss', says 'A girl was running down the hill.' 'watch-the-hill' describes the same beat as 'Eli watched the girl run closer down the hill' and 'He could wave first, or wait for her to speak' - dropping the -ing form at the one new passage inserted into this exact scene. Since this passage exists purely to give 'look-at-the-moss' a second choice, it is a natural, low-risk place to keep 'running' rather than paraphrase it away (for example 'Eli watched the girl, still running, come closer down the hill'). Please pass this to the narrative designer as a wording fix, not a story-logic fix.

Comprehension/craft note on the same 18 passages: seven of the nine round-2 (r6) passages share one template - one or two scene-setting sentences, then '[Eli/they] could [A], or [B]', where A and B are cosmetic (jump fast vs. ease down slowly; wave first vs. wait quietly; step in slowly vs. step in boldly) and both lead to the identical target with no difference in text, item, or consequence afterward. This satisfies the graph validator's 'two real choices' rule, but a reader who samples more than one of these will notice the repetition, and none of the nine advance plot, character or clue - which cuts against the brief's own instruction that reading should feel like an adventure rather than a lesson. This is a quality note, not a blocker: I'd ask the narrative designer to give at least a few of these a small narrative payoff (a sentence of world or character detail, as 'careful-hop' and 'last-look-at-the-gate' already do reasonably well) instead of a bare consequence-free fork, and to use the chance to pick up more word-set words per the two findings above.

Pre-existing, not introduced by r6, but worth re-stating since the stale r4 reviews should not be read as covering this: the closed-syllable word 'bus' occurs exactly once in the whole story (perWord in reports/literacy.r6.json), in 'the-gate' - 'A bus rumbled by without stopping.' A reader who chooses 'Squeeze through the gap after the cat' at the very first fork (into 'through-the-gap' instead of 'the-gate') never meets this word anywhere in the story. Likewise 'jumping' (ing set) is concentrated in 'stone-hop', one branch of the marsh detour, and is skippable via 'hop-stones' being avoided or via taking the stairs path instead of the marsh. The r4 literacy review (stories/jobs/job-20261020-the-cat-who-took-the-wro-fd6944/work/literacy-review.r4.json) already flagged both of these as known and allowed under the set-level rule ('each set should appear on every route', not each word); r6 does not change this, for better or worse. Flagging again only because I was asked for a full review of r6, not a diff from r4.

Carried over and unchanged from r4/r5, and correctly left out of scope per the r6 revision notes (which state the fix was single-choice passages only): three sentences remain one word over the brief's maxSentenceWords of 16. 'late-for-school': "Eli's library book had a map in it, and he was meant to show it in class." (17 words). 'frog-helped': "She was waiting at the start of the stairs, and she gave him a small, surprised smile." (17 words). 'home-too-soon': "He looked at his muddy shoes and thought of the marsh, the stairs and the dark hatch." (17 words). The automated sentence-length check only flags sentences over 20 words, so it reports ok; these are below that hard limit but above the brief's own stated target. Non-blocking, listed for completeness.

Limits of automated detection, restated for this revision: reports/literacy.r6.json and .md detect spelling patterns, not sound. For example the 'Digraph th' and 'Vowel team syllable' concept lists include 'anything' and 'nothing', which are compounds ('any'/'no' + 'thing'), not the targeted phonics pattern applied to a free base; the 'Suffix -ing' concept count (51 tokens) is a general spelling-pattern count across the whole story and is larger than, and partly independent of, the specific six-word ing-word-set the brief asks for. Syllable counts are estimates from vowel groups, not from how the words actually sound. None of this report, and nothing in this review, substitutes for a qualified human literacy or structured-literacy reviewer confirming decodability for the child's own program; my review is recorded with reviewer.kind 'ai-agent' and does not satisfy the human literacy review the publication policy requires.
